section.title: Godliness with Contentment
section.sectionRationale: Paul addresses servants and masters, then exposes false teachers who treat godliness as a way to get rich. Over against them he sets the true wealth: godliness with contentment is great gain. We brought nothing into the world and can take nothing out, so those who crave riches fall into ruin, for the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil.
section.thesis: Real gain is not money but godliness joined to contentment; the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil that pierces the greedy with many sorrows, while the godly rest content in God with food and covering.
section.frameNote: Three movements: honorable service under masters; the exposure of teachers who see godliness as a means of gain; and the great gain of godliness with contentment against the peril of loving money.

units.label: Serving with honor
units.note: so God's name is not discredited

verses.text: All who are under the {{zygos|yoke}} of slavery should regard their masters as fully worthy of honor, so that God’s name and our teaching will not be discredited.

Those who have believing masters should not show disrespect because they are brothers, but should serve them all the more, since those receiving their good service are beloved believers. Teach and encourage these principles.

units.label: Reject false doctrines
units.note: godliness is not a way to get rich

verses.text: If anyone teaches another doctrine and disagrees with the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and with godly teaching,
he is conceited and understands nothing. Instead, he has an unhealthy interest in controversies and disputes about words, out of which come envy, strife, abusive talk, evil suspicions,
and constant friction between men of depraved mind who are devoid of the truth. These men regard godliness as a means of {{porismos|gain}}.
Of course, {{eusebeia|godliness}} with {{autarkeia|contentment}} is great gain.
For we brought nothing into the world, so we cannot carry anything out of it.
But if we have food and clothing, we will be content with these.
Those who want to be rich, however, fall into temptation and become ensnared by many foolish and harmful desires that plunge them into ruin and destruction.
For the {{philargyria|love of money}} is the root of all kinds of evil. By craving it, some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows.

zygos.gloss: A yoke, the wooden bar laid across the neck of working animals, and by extension the burden of servitude. Bondservants under the yoke of slavery are to honor their masters so that the gospel is not slandered, showing the transforming power of faith even in hard circumstances.

porismos.gloss: A means of gain, a way of making money. The false teachers treat godliness as porismos, a business to enrich themselves. Paul overturns the word in verse 6: godliness truly is great gain, but joined to contentment, not to greed.

eusebeia.gloss: Godliness, reverence for God lived out, a key word of the Pastoral Epistles. The false teachers prize it only as a path to profit, but real godliness, paired with contentment, is the great gain, valuable now and forever, unlike money that cannot be carried out of the world.

autarkeia.gloss: Contentment, self-sufficiency, a settled satisfaction independent of circumstances. For Paul it is not stoic self-reliance but rest in God's provision, being satisfied with food and covering. Joined to godliness, it turns a modest life into great gain.

philargyria.gloss: The love of money, literally love of silver. Paul calls it a root of all kinds of evil. It is not money itself but the craving for it that leads people astray, luring some away from the faith and piercing them with many sorrows.

basic.context: Paul tells Christian servants to honor their masters so the gospel is not discredited, and to serve believing masters all the more. He then exposes false teachers who are proud, quarrelsome, and see godliness as a way to make money. Against them he sets the truth: godliness with contentment is great gain. We come with nothing and leave with nothing, so craving riches leads to ruin, because the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil.
basic.hermeneutics: The instruction to servants speaks into a real social setting; its enduring principle is that faith transforms how we work and relate, guarding the gospel's reputation. The teaching on money is directly prescriptive: contentment is the mark of godliness, and the love of money is a spiritual danger to be fled.
basic.originalLanguages: Servants under the zygos, yoke, honor their masters. False teachers treat godliness as porismos, a means of gain, but real eusebeia, godliness, with autarkeia, contentment, is great gain. The philargyria, love of money, is a root of all kinds of evil.
basic.typology: Contentment with food and covering recalls Israel gathering daily manna, trusting God's provision, and points to Christ who bids us seek first the kingdom and trust our Father for daily bread. The true riches are found in Him.
basic.christ: Sound teaching is measured by the words of our Lord Jesus Christ. He, though rich, became poor so that we through His poverty might become rich, embodying the great gain of godliness that no money can buy. To wander after wealth is to wander from the faith that is in Him.
basic.god: God's name is at stake in how His people work and handle money. He is the giver of every good thing and the true treasure that makes contentment possible. He warns that the love of money competes with love for Him and pierces the heart that chases it.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 13 says be content with what you have, for God will never leave you. Matthew 6 warns you cannot serve God and money. Philippians 4 tells of learning contentment in every circumstance.
basic.oneStory: From manna in the wilderness to the treasure of the kingdom, God has taught His people to trust Him rather than riches. Here He exposes greed dressed as religion and calls His people to contentment in Him. It is part of His long work of freeing hearts from idols to find their gain in Christ.

context.literary:
The passage is one sentence of instruction followed by one long argument, and the argument is built as a pair of contrasts. Verses 1 and 2 belong to the pattern of household teaching found in several letters. Verses 3 to 5 are a single sentence in Greek, a portrait of the false teacher that begins with what he does, teaches another doctrine, moves to what he is, conceited and understanding nothing, and then to what he produces, envy, strife, abusive talk, evil suspicions and friction. The list is a chain of cause and effect. Bad teaching grows in a sick mind, and a sick mind produces a sick community.

The hinge is verse 6. The false teachers regard godliness as a way of gain, and Paul takes the same word and turns it. Godliness is indeed gain, great gain, but only when joined with contentment. The next two verses supply the argument. We brought nothing, we shall take nothing, so food and clothing are enough. Verse 9 and verse 10 then reverse the sentence by describing the opposite appetite. 'Those who want to be rich' are trapped, plunged, and wounded. The verbs form a descent: temptation, snare, many desires, ruin, destruction, wandering, piercing.

There is a pattern of imagery. Verses 9 and 10 use a hunter's trap, a sinking ship and a spear. The man who wants more finds he is caught, drowned and pierced. The opening verses also have a pattern, since verse 1 worries about the name of God and the teaching being discredited and verse 2 about believing masters, so the first lines show that the passage is concerned with how the gospel looks from outside and how it is lived inside.
context.historical:
Slavery in the Roman world was pervasive, and in a large city like Ephesus a substantial share of the population were slaves. Some were servants of great houses and held trusted roles, while others did hard manual labour. Many first Christians were slaves, and a believing slave in a pagan household and a believing slave in a Christian household each faced a different temptation. The first might hope that faith would excuse him from service. The second might presume on the fact that the master was a brother. Paul addresses both. Elsewhere he gives parallel instructions, Ephesians 6:5 to 9, Colossians 3:22 to 4:1 and Titus 2:9 to 10, and he asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as a beloved brother, Philemon 1:16. In this letter he lists slave traders among those whom the law condemns, 1 Timothy 1:10. The church was not the author of the institution, and its message undermined the institution's spiritual basis from within, as Galatians 3:28 shows.

The false teachers who treated godliness as a means of gain would not have looked out of place in Ephesus. Travelling teachers who charged fees were a familiar part of the Greek world, and Ephesus itself was a wealthy trading city whose craftsmen lived off the worship of Artemis, Acts 19:24 to 27. Demetrius says outright that the business is the source of their prosperity, Acts 19:25. Paul's warning has a local colour: religion connected to money was an old story in this city.

The word contentment was familiar to moral philosophers, who prized a self-sufficiency that needed nothing. Paul takes the word and gives it a new ground, since he can say he has learned to be content in every situation, and the strength comes from Christ, Philippians 4:11 to 13.
context.canonical:
The thought of verse 7 is old. Job says he came naked from his mother's womb and will return naked, Job 1:21, and Ecclesiastes 5:15 says a man departs as he arrived and takes nothing for his labour in his hands. Psalm 49:16 to 17 makes the same point about the rich who die and cannot take their wealth with them. Proverbs 30:8 prays for neither poverty nor riches, and asks only for the bread that is one's portion, and that prayer is the nearest Old Testament parallel to 'food and clothing.'

In the teaching of Jesus the same warning is central. He says that one cannot serve both God and money, Matthew 6:24, that one's life does not consist in the abundance of possessions, Luke 12:15, and He tells the story of the rich fool whose life was required that night, Luke 12:16 to 21. Hebrews 13:5 joins contentment and the love of money in a sentence that is close to verses 6 to 10. It tells readers to keep their lives free from the love of money and to be content, because God has said He will never leave them. James 5:1 to 6 rebukes rich oppressors, and Colossians 3:5 says that greed is idolatry.

The warning about false teachers who exploit the church is found in Titus 1:11, where those who teach for shameful gain are named, in 2 Peter 2:3, and in Jude 11, which speaks of rushing headlong into the error of Balaam. The theme continues through 2 Timothy 3:2, where people will be lovers of money, and into Revelation 3:17, where the church that says it is rich needs nothing.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wanted slaves in the church to see their work as a witness. If a believing slave despised his master, the world would blame the faith, and the name of God and the teaching would be spoken against. The point of the instruction is the reputation of the gospel, not the approval of the institution. He also wanted slaves of believing masters to serve better, not worse, because the master was a brother.

The longer part of the passage is aimed at those who would use the church for profit and at those in the church who might admire them. Paul wanted Timothy to be able to say that quarrelsome, clever teaching that makes money is not just poor teaching, it is a sign of a diseased mind. He also wanted the believers to hear, in plain words, what actually satisfies. The answer is not poverty and not wealth but godliness with contentment, a life that has what it needs because it has God. The warning about craving riches is a warning about a process: it begins with wanting, it ends in ruin, and some on the way have wandered from the faith.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The instruction to slaves describes how believers lived within the social order they found, and it is addressed to people with no power to change it. It is not a divine endorsement of slavery. Paul condemns the trade in people in 1 Timothy 1:10, and tells Philemon to receive a slave as a brother. Applying the passage today means asking what it says about work and witness, not copying the arrangement. Employees and employers can take from it the principles that faith improves work, that fellow believers must not trade on the relationship, and that the church's name is at stake in ordinary labour.

The teaching on money is more directly prescriptive. The statements that godliness with contentment is great gain and that the love of money is a source of evils are not tied to a particular culture. They describe the way the human heart works anywhere. Paul does not say that money is evil, nor that having it is sinful, since he goes on in verses 17 to 19 to instruct the rich. He says the craving for it ensnares. The passage also does not promise that godly living will make a person rich; it denies that godliness is a method for gaining wealth.

debates.question: Does this passage endorse slavery?

views.label: No, it works within the institution and undermines its basis
views.case: Paul speaks to the people actually in the pews, who could not end the system alone. He condemns slave trading in 1 Timothy 1:10, calls a master and a slave brothers in Philemon 1:16, tells masters in Ephesians 6:9 that they have a Master in heaven who shows no favouritism, and says in Galatians 3:28 that in Christ there is neither slave nor free. On this view the instruction is realistic guidance for a situation that the gospel would eventually dissolve.

views.label: It reflects the culture and does not set a norm
views.case: Others stress that Paul never calls the institution wrong in so many words, and that his advice is shaped by what was possible. They say the passage describes how believers lived and does not prescribe it for other times, while the larger direction of Scripture opposes treating people as property.

views.label: It is a call to witness inside unjust structures
views.case: Some emphasise that the main concern is how the faith looks from outside, verse 1, and that the point carries to any situation where a believer works under unfair authority, while still leaving room for freedom to be taken where it can be, as 1 Corinthians 7:21 suggests.

debates.bearing: None of these readings sees the passage as approval of owning people. All agree the focus is how believers behave and how the name of God is regarded, and the wider witness of the New Testament leads to the dignity of every person.

debates.question: Is the love of money 'the root' or 'a root' of all kinds of evil in verse 10?

views.label: A root of all kinds of evils
views.case: The Greek has no article before 'root,' so it can be read 'a root,' and many versions translate it so. Paul does not say that greed is the only source of evil, only that it can feed every kind. The plural 'evils' suggests it is a root from which many sins grow.

views.label: The root, in a proverbial sense
views.case: Others take the sentence as a bold, proverbial statement in which the noun without the article is still definite in sense, like the saying that money is the source of all trouble. The point is the same: greed is dangerous at the base of conduct.

debates.bearing: Either way, Paul says the love of money, not money itself, is the source. The sentence is a warning about desire, and the verse that follows shows how it works in human lives, in wandering and wounds.

debates.question: What does 'wandered away from the faith' mean in verse 10?

views.label: Believers who lose their faith
views.case: The verb describes people who were once inside the faith and have gone astray, and the passage warns that the danger is real. This reading takes the warning at its plain force and fits 1 Timothy 4:1 and 1:19.

views.label: Those who professed but never truly believed
views.case: Others hold that those who wander show they were never fully of the faith, as 1 John 2:19 says of those who left. The warning then addresses a professing community and tests reality.

debates.bearing: Both read the verse as a serious warning. Whatever the final view of perseverance, the instruction is the same: flee the love of money, as verse 11 says, and hold to the faith.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word of the passage is zygos, the yoke, the wooden beam that bound two animals together, and by extension the burden of servitude. Paul says 'under the yoke of slavery,' using the common word doulos for the slave. In verse 2 the warning not to 'show disrespect' uses kataphroneo, to think down on, to look down on, and it is the same verb that Paul uses of Timothy's youth in 4:12 when he tells the church not to despise him. The pairing suggests a theme: despising people because of their station, or despising masters because they are brothers, is the same mistake.

Verse 3 introduces the false teacher by the verb heterodidaskaleo, to teach something different, which also stands in 1:3. The standard of sound teaching is described as 'sound words,' hygiainontes logoi, healthy words, from the same root as the English hygiene. Paul uses the medical image throughout the pastoral letters, 2 Timothy 1:13 and Titus 2:1. In verse 4 the false teacher is called conceited, from typhoo, a perfect passive participle that means 'has been puffed up,' and the root has to do with smoke. Paul uses it of the novice overseer in 3:6. The contrast follows at once with a medical word, nosoo, to be sick. The false teacher has 'an unhealthy interest' in controversies, which literally means he is diseased with them, and the object is 'semantics,' logomachia, a battle over words. In verse 5, the 'depraved mind' is corrupted, and the men are 'deprived of the truth,' a perfect participle again, which says that the truth has been taken away from them.

In verse 6 the word translated 'contentment' is autarkeia. The word was prized in Greek moral thought for the person who needs nothing from outside. Paul uses the adjective of himself in Philippians 4:11 and the noun of God's provision in 2 Corinthians 9:8, where God makes grace abound so that you will have all sufficiency in all things. The ground of sufficiency has moved from the self to God. In verse 8, 'we will be content' is the verb arkeo, used in Hebrews 13:5. The word for 'clothing' is skepasma, which means covering, and can include shelter as well as clothes, so Paul's list of necessities is very short.

Verse 9 changes the verb. The people 'who want to be rich' are boulomai, they deliberately wish for it. The trap is pagis, a snare for catching birds or animals, the same word used for the devil's trap in 3:7 and 2 Timothy 2:26. The ruin is described by the verb bythizo, to sink, used of the boats that began to sink in Luke 5:7. In verse 10 the love of money is philargyria, from philos and argyrion, love of silver. The word for 'craving' is oregomai, to stretch out toward, used in 3:1 for aspiring to oversight. The final result is odyne, pains, a word for deep distress as in Romans 9:2.

typology.fulfillment: In the wilderness the people were told to gather as much as each needed, and those who gathered much had no excess and those who gathered little had no shortfall, Exodus 16:18. They were taught, Moses later says, that man does not live on bread alone but on every word from the mouth of the LORD, Deuteronomy 8:3. Paul's 'food and clothing' stands in this line. In Christ the lesson reaches its centre: He is the bread of life, John 6:35, and taught His followers to ask for daily bread, Matthew 6:11. The type falls short because manna fed the body only, and the true bread gives eternal life, John 6:49 to 51.

Achan saw a cloak, silver and a bar of gold, and says he coveted them and took them, Joshua 7:21. His desire brought ruin on himself and on Israel. The pattern of verse 9, desire, snare, ruin, is lived out in a single tent. In Christ the pattern is answered by one who had every right to take and gave up all, Philippians 2:6 to 8. The type falls short in one way. Achan's sin is visible and punished; the love of money in the church may be quiet and respectable, as Gehazi's greed was in 2 Kings 5:20 to 27, which makes Paul's warning all the more urgent.

The slave who serves well in verse 1 anticipates the true Servant. Isaiah's servant of the LORD bears the burdens of others, Isaiah 53:11, and in Christ the servant's role is taken at its deepest. He emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, Philippians 2:7, and said He came not to be served but to serve and to give His life as a ransom, Mark 10:45. The believing slave who works well for a brother is following the pattern of the One who became a servant for us. The type is limited because Christ's service was by choice, and He also frees the slaves of sin, John 8:36.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ first through 'the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ' in verse 3. The standard by which every teacher is measured is not a school of thought but the actual words of Jesus. It means that the teaching of the church is a matter of listening to someone who spoke. The false teacher is not simply wrong about a doctrine; he disagrees with the Lord Himself. The words of Jesus on money, 'You cannot serve both God and money,' Matthew 6:24, and, 'Watch out! Guard yourselves against every form of greed,' Luke 12:15, are the sound words that verses 6 to 10 draw out.

It leads to Christ through contrast of wealth. The false teachers see godliness as a way to gain, and Jesus is the one who gave up gain. Paul says elsewhere that though He was rich, yet for our sakes He became poor, so that through His poverty we might become rich, 2 Corinthians 8:9. He had no place to lay His head, Matthew 8:20. He told a rich man that he lacked one thing, to sell what he had and follow Him, Mark 10:21, and the man went away sad. The Lord who calls His people to be content with food and clothing is the Lord who lived that way, and He offers what money cannot buy.

It leads to Christ through the servant. The Son took the form of a servant, Philippians 2:7, and said He came to serve and give His life, Mark 10:45. The slave who works honestly, even under an unjust master, shares in the pattern of the One who served those who did not deserve it. Peter makes the link explicit when he speaks to servants and points them to Christ's suffering and example, 1 Peter 2:18 to 21.

It leads to Christ through the question of gain. 'What does it profit a man to gain the whole world, yet forfeit his soul?' Jesus asked, Mark 8:36. Paul's phrase 'great gain' is an answer to the same question. Real gain is to know Christ and to be found in Him, as Paul writes in Philippians 3:7 to 9, where he counts everything as loss for the sake of Christ. The one who has Christ has what the love of money promises and cannot deliver.

A caution keeps the reading sound. The passage does not say that Jesus is poor and that therefore believers must be, and it does not make every servant a type of Christ. What it says is that godliness, which is a life in union with Him, joined with a heart that needs nothing more than He supplies, is great gain.
study.god:
The first thing the passage shows is that God's name is at stake in ordinary life. The reason Paul gives for the slaves' respect is that 'God's name and our teaching' might not be discredited. The reputation of God is bound up with the conduct of His people, in workplaces and households. It is a sobering thought that a believer's attitude to a boss can speak well or ill of the Lord.

It shows God as the standard of truth. Paul says the false teacher understands nothing and is devoid of the truth. This is not abuse, it is a statement that truth is a gift from God and that without Him the mind loses its way. Sound words are healthy words, and God's word is the food of a healthy mind. God's character shapes how teaching is judged: not by how clever it is, but by what it produces, whether love, peace and truth, or envy, strife and suspicion.

It shows God as the sufficient One. The word autarkeia is used of God's provision in 2 Corinthians 9:8, and Paul's argument is that those who have God have enough. The passage says we brought nothing and we take nothing, which reminds the reader that all is received. God is the giver of every good thing, as verse 17 later adds, and He supplies food and clothing as He supplied manna. Contentment is thus not a mood but a way of trusting that God is a good provider.

It shows God as one who warns before He judges. The sequence of temptation, snare, ruin and destruction, wandering and sorrows is spelled out so that people might step back. The love of money is not a minor flaw; Jesus says it is a rival master, Matthew 6:24. God cares enough to say so plainly, and the warning itself is grace.

It shows God as the one whom the heart is meant to desire. Verse 10 speaks of craving, a reaching out. The human heart was made to reach for something. The passage implies that the love of money is a misplaced form of the desire for God, and that the only remedy is to have the right object. Hence the call in verse 11 to pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, perseverance and gentleness.

For worship, the passage invites the believer to give thanks for food and clothing, to work as before the Lord, and to find joy not in what is stored but in the God who gives.

crossReferences.note: Job says he came naked from his mother's womb and will return naked, and that the LORD gave and the LORD has taken away. The sentence behind 1 Timothy 6:7 is here, and it shows that holding possessions loosely is possible in the middle of loss, and not only in prosperity.

A man departs as he came, and takes nothing of his labour in his hands. The Preacher's observation is the same as Paul's. The argument is that wealth cannot go with us, so it cannot be the final good of life.

Agur asks for neither poverty nor riches, only the bread that is his portion. The prayer is the closest Old Testament match to 'food and clothing' and shows that the wisdom of contentment is a long tradition in Scripture.

Jesus does not say money is a tool that can be mishandled; He gives it a master's place, a rival that competes for the same loyalty God asks. Paul's picture of those who crave riches drifting from the faith, verse 10, is this sentence acted out in a life.

Jesus warns against every form of greed and says one's life does not consist in the abundance of possessions. The saying introduces the rich fool and gives the principle behind Paul's teaching on gain and contentment.

The writer tells readers to keep their lives free from the love of money and to be content, because God has said He will never leave them. The reason for contentment is the presence of God, and this gives the positive side of 1 Timothy 6:6 to 10.

Paul says he has learned to be content regardless of his circumstances. The verse shows that contentment is learned, and it comes from a source beyond circumstances, which is verse 13, the strength given by Christ.
Paul tells believers to put to death greed, which is idolatry. This links the love of money in 1 Timothy 6:10 to the first commandment, since greed gives to wealth the trust that belongs to God.
Slaves are to obey earthly masters with respect and sincerity of heart, as they would obey Christ. This is the parallel to 1 Timothy 6:1 and adds the motive, to serve the Lord in serving the master.

Paul sends Onesimus back no longer as a slave but better than a slave, as a beloved brother. The verse shows how the gospel changes a relationship from within, and explains why verse 2 tells slaves not to presume upon a believing master.

Though Christ was rich, for our sakes He became poor, so that through His poverty we might become rich. The verse gives the deepest answer to the question of gain, because it describes a wealth that cannot be spent or lost.

study.oneStory:
At the beginning the man and woman had everything they needed, and the first temptation was to want what God had withheld, Genesis 3:6. The love of money is the old story in its modern coat. In the wilderness God fed Israel with manna and taught them to trust Him for each day, Exodus 16:18, and the people grumbled all the same. Through the prophets and the Proverbs the lesson is repeated: do not set your heart on riches, Psalm 62:10, and Agur's prayer asks only for what he needs, Proverbs 30:8.

The passage fits into the larger story of the people of God as those who are being freed from idols. Paul calls greed idolatry in Colossians 3:5, and the passage shows how it works in practice, drawing a person down through desire to ruin. The church at Ephesus lived in a city whose trade depended on a goddess, Acts 19:24 to 27, and the temptation to treat religion as a business was real.

The passage also shows the gospel at work in the structure of daily life. The slave and the master, who in Roman society stood at the opposite ends of the social order, are said to be brothers in the church, and the result is a quiet but lasting change. In time the very idea that one person can own another would be challenged by the same message, and Galatians 3:28 is the seed of that.

The story is moving toward a place where the contrast between gain and loss is resolved. Jesus says that where treasure is, there the heart will be also, Matthew 6:19 to 21, and invites His people to store up treasure in heaven. In the new creation there will be no more curse, and the servants of God will serve Him and reign, Revelation 22:3 to 5. The contentment that is learned in a world of want is a rehearsal for a life in which God Himself is the portion, and the want is gone.

quiz.q: Why are Christian servants told to honor their masters?

options.text: So that God's name and the church's teaching will not be discredited.
options.note: Verse 1 gives the gospel's reputation as the reason.

options.text: Because slavery is a good and permanent institution.
options.note: Paul addresses believers within the system, not commending it; the aim is the gospel's witness.

options.text: Because masters always deserve it on their own merits.
options.note: The motive given is the honor of God's name, not the masters' merit.

options.text: So they can earn their freedom by good behavior.
options.note: The stated goal is the gospel's reputation, not earning freedom.

quiz.q: How does Paul describe teachers who use religion for profit?

options.text: Conceited, quarrelsome, and regarding godliness as a means of gain.
options.note: Verses 4 and 5 expose their pride and greed.

options.text: Wise leaders worth imitating.
options.note: They are the opposite of what to imitate; Paul condemns them.

options.text: Sincere but slightly mistaken.
options.note: Paul calls them depraved in mind and devoid of the truth, not merely mistaken.

options.text: Harmless eccentrics.
options.note: They breed envy, strife, and friction; they are far from harmless.

quiz.q: What does Paul say is great gain?

options.text: Godliness with contentment.
options.note: Verse 6 names godliness joined to contentment as great gain.

options.text: Godliness that produces wealth.
options.note: That is the false teachers' view; Paul pairs godliness with contentment, not riches.

options.text: Wealth accumulated through hard work.
options.note: We can carry nothing out; wealth is not the gain Paul commends.

options.text: Freedom from all responsibility.
options.note: The gain is godliness with contentment, not escape from duty.

quiz.q: What reason does Paul give for contentment in verses 7 and 8?

options.text: We brought nothing into the world and can carry nothing out; food and clothing suffice.
options.note: Verses 7 and 8 ground contentment in this reality.

options.text: Because possessions last forever.
options.note: The opposite; we cannot take anything out, which is why we should be content.

options.text: Because poverty is holier than provision.
options.note: Paul is content with food and clothing, not idealizing poverty itself.

options.text: Because God does not care about our needs.
options.note: God provides; contentment rests on His provision, not His indifference.

quiz.q: What does Paul say about the love of money?

options.text: It is a root of all kinds of evil that has led some away from the faith.
options.note: Verse 10 names the love of money, not money itself, as the danger.

options.text: Money itself is the single root of every evil.
options.note: A common misquotation; Paul specifies the love of money and a root of all kinds of evil.

options.text: Wealth is always sinful to possess.
options.note: The peril is the craving for money; verses 17 to 19 treat wealth as a stewardship.

options.text: Money has no spiritual danger at all.
options.note: Paul warns it can pierce people with many sorrows and draw them from the faith.

questions: Paul says our work can either commend or discredit the gospel. How does your conduct at work reflect on the God you claim to serve?
The false teachers saw godliness as a way to get rich. Where might you be tempted to treat faith as a means to some other gain?
Godliness with contentment is great gain. What would genuine contentment with food and covering look like in your life this year?
We bring nothing in and take nothing out. How does that reality reshape the way you hold your possessions and plans?
The love of money pierces people with many sorrows. Where do you sense that craving pulling at your heart, and how will you flee it?

translationNotes.note: The BSB footnote notes that some manuscripts add Withdraw yourself from such, a later reading not in the earliest texts.
The BSB footnote records the variant so certainly for so, a minor difference among manuscript families.
The love of money renders philargyria, love of silver; Paul says it is a root of all kinds of evil, not that money itself is the root of every evil.
